A sect is a group of people who share a specific set of beliefs or practices — and whose shared beliefs set them apart from a larger, more established group they originally came from or exist in contrast to.

Think of it this way: imagine a large religion with millions of followers. Over time, some people within that religion come to believe that the mainstream is getting things wrong — maybe they're misinterpreting a holy text, following the wrong rituals, or straying from the "true" path. These people form their own tighter, more distinct group around their version of the belief. That breakaway group is a sect.

A sect is always a subgroup — it exists in relation to something bigger. You don't call an entire major religion a sect. You call a branch, a splinter group, or a faction within it a sect.

Members of a sect are united by:

  • Shared belief: They agree on a specific interpretation of doctrine, scripture, or ideology that the broader group does not share.
  • A sense of distinction: They typically believe they hold the correct or purer version of the belief, while others have drifted or gone astray.
  • Shared practice: Often, they follow particular rituals, customs, or codes of conduct that mark them as different from outsiders.
  • A defined boundary: There is usually a clear sense of "us" (the sect) vs. "them" (the larger group or mainstream society).

The word sect appears most commonly in religious contexts, but it extends further.

In religion — this is by far the most common use. Almost every major religion has sects within it.

  • Islam has two major sects: Sunni and Shia. They share the core of the Islamic faith but differ on questions of leadership and certain practices that go back to the early history of Islam.
  • Christianity has hundreds of sects — groups like Quakers, Seventh-day Adventists, and many others who broke away from mainstream churches over matters of doctrine or worship.
  • Hinduism contains many sects, such as Vaishnavism and Shaivism, which differ in which deity they regard as supreme and how they worship.
  • Buddhism too has distinct sects, like Theravada and Mahayana, with different teachings and practices.

In politics — a sect can refer to a small, tight-knit faction within a larger political movement, one that holds more extreme or distinct views than the mainstream of that movement.

In philosophy — historically, philosophical schools of thought (like the Stoics, the Epicureans) were sometimes called sects, since they were groups that gathered around specific thinkers and their doctrines.
The tone and connotation of the word

This is important to understand: the word sect is not entirely neutral. Its tone can vary depending on who uses it and in what context.

Used neutrally — academics, historians, and journalists often use "sect" as a plain descriptive term, without judgment. When a historian says "the Shia sect," they simply mean this branch of Islam.

Used with a negative shade — in everyday language, calling a group a "sect" can imply it is marginal, suspicious, rigid, or fanatical. It carries a subtle suggestion that the group is deviant from what most consider normal or acceptable. This is why members of such groups often prefer to call themselves a "church," a "denomination," or a "tradition" rather than a "sect" — because "sect" can feel like an outsider's label, one that dismisses or belittles them.

So the same group might be called a "sect" by critics and a "denomination" or "community" by its own members or sympathizers. The choice of word reveals the speaker's attitude.

Understanding "sect" becomes sharper when you compare it to related words.

Sect vs. denomination
A denomination is a larger, well-established, socially recognized branch of a religion — like Catholics, Baptists, or Lutherans within Christianity. Denominations are mainstream and respected. A sect is typically smaller, newer, more marginal, and viewed with more suspicion. The line between the two can blur over time — what starts as a sect may eventually grow into a fully accepted denomination.

Sect vs. cult
This is the most important distinction. A cult is a far more extreme version. Cults are usually characterized by:

  • An all-powerful, charismatic leader who demands absolute loyalty
  • Extreme psychological control over members
  • Isolation of members from family, friends, and outside society
  • Exit being difficult or dangerous

A sect does not necessarily have any of these features. Members of a sect typically live normal lives in the wider world. The word "sect" is much milder than "cult." However, in casual speech, people sometimes use "sect" loosely to describe what is technically a cult, so the two words do overlap in informal usage.

Sect vs. religion
A religion is the whole, the full tradition — Islam, Christianity, Hinduism. A sect is a part of it, a branch. You would never call Islam itself a sect; you would call Sunni Islam or Shia Islam sects within Islam.
A few quick examples in sentences

• After a disagreement over leadership, a small sect broke away from the main church and started holding separate gatherings.
  • The Amish are a Christian sect known for their rejection of modern technology and simple, traditional way of life.
  • The political movement eventually fractured, with one sect pushing for immediate revolution and another preferring gradual reform.
  • Historians have documented dozens of Jewish sects that existed in ancient Palestine, each with its own interpretation of the law.

A sect is a distinct subgroup — most often religious, sometimes political or philosophical — that has separated itself from a larger body through its own specific beliefs or practices. It sees itself as holding a truer, purer, or more correct understanding than the mainstream. The word is factually descriptive but carries a mild negative undertone in everyday use, suggesting something marginal or unorthodox. It is less extreme than a cult and less established than a denomination, sitting somewhere between the two on the spectrum of organized belief groups.
